analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income taxes with a flat 17% tax on wages and business income and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: This flat-tax bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced in May 1999 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would scrap the graduated income tax and replace it with a single 17% tax on cash wages and business income. It taxes only wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment benefits — so capital gains, dividends, and interest income would owe nothing. It repeals the estate and gift tax, the alternative minimum tax, and all tax credits, and it would let employers take money out of pension plans without penalty. To hold down the lost revenue, it caps total federal spending, requires a three-fifths vote of Congress to raise any tax rate or shrink the standard deduction, and ends the spending authority of most federal programs unless Congress reauthorizes them.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest gains go to the wealthiest households: their wages would be taxed at 17% instead of 39.6%, their investment income (capital gains, dividends, interest) would be untaxed entirely, and the estate tax — which falls only on large estates — disappears. Businesses get a 17-20% tax on profits after deducting wages and input costs, replacing the corporate income tax. Lower-wage workers also benefit from very large standard deductions ($22,000 for couples, $11,000 for singles, $15,000 per child), which would take many families off the tax rolls, and everyone gains from simpler filing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, large estates, and businesses

how_it_helps.text: It replaces all individual income tax rates with a single flat 17% rate, which cuts the top rate from 39.6% and would give the biggest dollar savings to people with the highest incomes.

Taxable income is defined to include only cash wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, so capital gains, dividends, and interest would owe no federal tax — a change that overwhelmingly benefits households living on investment income.
It repeals the estate and gift tax (retroactive to deaths after 1996), which only affects the largest estates.

Large standard deductions — $22,000 for a married couple, $11,000 for a single person, plus $15,000 per dependent — plus inflation adjustments would shield most low- and middle-income wage earners from federal income tax and make filing far simpler.
It repeals the alternative minimum tax and all tax credits, eliminating two of the most complicated parts of the code for ordinary filers.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would collect far less revenue, and the bill's spending title shows where the difference would come from: hard caps on total spending, a rule ending the spending authority of 'unearned entitlements' (defined to exclude only Social Security, Medicare, and veterans and retirement benefits) and of every other program unless Congress affirmatively reauthorizes them, and automatic across-the-board cuts if spending exceeds the caps. Programs and the people who rely on them would bear that. Separately, governments and tax-exempt employers would owe a new 20% tax on the value of noncash benefits they provide employees — including health insurance — which would pressure those benefits.

drawbacks.text: Removing all tax on capital gains, dividends, and interest, while taxing wages at 17%, shifts the tax burden away from income that flows mostly to wealthy households and toward income from work; the CRS summary shows taxable income is defined to exclude investment income entirely.

The bill repeals pension nondiscrimination rules that stop plans from favoring highly paid executives, repeals limits on contributions, and allows employers to pull excess assets out of pension plans without paying the excise tax that currently applies — changes that weaken protections for rank-and-file workers' retirement security.

The revenue loss would have to be offset somehow: the bill's own spending title ends the spending authority of most federal programs unless Congress reauthorizes them and imposes hard spending caps with automatic cuts, which ordinary people who rely on federal programs would feel directly.

A new 20% tax on noncash compensation would apply to government and tax-exempt employers, taxing the value of benefits like health coverage provided to their employees — a cost those employers would face for benefits other employers' workers receive tax-free.

Requiring a three-fifths vote to raise tax rates, cut the standard deduction, or create any tax benefit would let a minority of lawmakers block future tax changes permanently, which supporters call protection and critics call a lock-in of whatever structure first wins.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification is real: filing under this system would be dramatically easier, and the large standard deductions would genuinely help low- and middle-wage workers. But the bill's largest dollar benefits clearly flow upward — untaxed investment income, a 39.6%-to-17% top-rate cut, and estate tax repeal — and the bill itself supplies the mechanism for absorbing the revenue loss through spending caps and mandatory reauthorization of programs. Whether the flat rate plus deductions is a net win for a given family depends on where they sit; whether the overall package is revenue-neutral is not established in the bill text, and its sponsors' answer was to sunset programs rather than raise the rate.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Shelby introduced the bill in May 1999 and the Senate sent it straight to the Finance Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Shelby introduced the Freedom and Fairness Restoration Act of 1997 (his title from the prior Congress) in the Senate on May 13, 1999, joined by Senator Craig.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced, and the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill expired without ever reaching the Senate floor or either chamber's voters.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal programs were untouched, the estate tax stayed in place, and the tax code kept taxing investment income — so the status quo, with its existing protections for program beneficiaries and progressive rates, persisted. Nobody gained new benefits; high earners simply did not get the tax cut the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo, and federal programs

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on May 13, 1999.

for.name: Sen. Larry Craig
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chaired by Sen. William Roth, R-DE)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 13, 1999 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it; the bill died in the committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so the record shows no party split — only that a single-cosponsor bill from the majority's own party stalled in a committee also chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill cuts their top tax rate from 39.6% to 17%, removes all tax on capital gains, dividends, and interest, and repeals the estate tax entirely. That revenue would have been made up, under the bill's own terms, through spending caps and program terminations that fall on services ordinary people use.

The corporate income tax is replaced with a 17-20% tax on business profit after deducting wages and input costs, and pension nondiscrimination and contribution rules are repealed. These are gains for employers that come alongside weaker retirement protections for their workers.

Investment income — capital gains, dividends, interest — would be completely untaxed, and financial intermediation is taxed only on the value of the service provided. This channel of the bill directs its largest benefit toward financial income.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local governments; tax-exempt employers
industries.note: A new 20% tax would fall on the value of noncash benefits (such as health insurance) these employers provide their employees, and the bill's spending caps and reauthorization rules would squeeze government programs and the workers and beneficiaries who depend on them.

Workers gain from untaxed retirement-plan contributions and distributions being the only taxed channel, but the bill repeals the nondiscrimination, coverage, and top-heavy rules that keep plans from tilting toward executives, and lets employers reclaim excess pension assets penalty-free.
